# Introduction

`dbsnR` provides a structured workflow to download, cache, inspect,
merge, search, filter, crop, analyse, visualise, and export spatial data
from the Italian Database di Sintesi Nazionale (DBSN).

The package is designed to simplify repetitive operations across
provincial DBSN geodatabases while keeping the resulting spatial
objects compatible with the standard R spatial ecosystem.

This vignette presents a complete workflow, from provincial DBSN
datasets stored in the local cache to spatial analysis, interactive
mapping, and export.

```{r}
library(dbsnR)
library(sf)
```

# Download provincial datasets

DBSN datasets can be downloaded and stored in the local `dbsnR` cache.

For example:

```{r}
dbsn_download("RI")
dbsn_download("AQ")
dbsn_download("RM")
```

Once downloaded, the datasets remain available in the local cache and
can be reused without downloading them again.

The cache location can be inspected with:

```{r}
dbsn_cache_dir()
```

The following workflow assumes that the required provincial datasets
are already available in the cache.

# Define the provinces

In this example, the analysis uses Rieti and the surrounding provinces.

```{r}
provinces <- c(
  "RI",
  "AP",
  "AQ",
  "PG",
  "RM",
  "TE",
  "TR",
  "VT"
)
```

# Explore available DBSN layers

`dbsn_layers()` inspects the geodatabases available in the local cache
without loading all spatial features into memory.

```{r}
layers <- dbsn_layers(
  province = provinces
)

head(layers)
```

The returned catalogue contains information such as:

- layer name;
- geometry type;
- number of provinces where the layer exists;
- province codes.

A detailed catalogue with one row for each layer/province combination
can also be requested.

```{r}
layers_detail <- dbsn_layers(
  province = provinces,
  details = TRUE
)

head(layers_detail)
```

# Inspect a DBSN layer

Before loading a potentially large spatial dataset, `dbsn_info()` can
be used to inspect a specific layer.

```{r}
dbsn_info(
  "bosco",
  province = provinces
)
```

This reports the number of features available for each province and
indicates whether the layer contains data.

A DBSN layer may exist inside a provincial geodatabase while containing
zero features.

For example:

```{r}
dbsn_info(
  "cascata",
  province = provinces
)
```

`dbsn_info()` distinguishes between available, empty, unavailable, and
unreadable layers.

# Merge provincial datasets

A single DBSN layer can be loaded and merged across several provinces.

```{r}
loc_sg <- dbsn_merge(
  layer = "loc_sg",
  province = provinces
)
```

The result is a standard `sf` object.

`dbsn_merge()` also adds information about the origin of each feature,
including the province and source geodatabase.

```{r}
table(loc_sg$province)
```

The coordinate reference system can be inspected with `sf`.

```{r}
st_crs(loc_sg)
```

# Search for a place

`dbsn_search()` searches attribute values within an `sf` layer.

Orvinio can be located in the merged `loc_sg` layer with:

```{r}
orvinio <- dbsn_search(
  x = loc_sg,
  pattern = "Orvinio"
)
```

The result remains an `sf` object and can therefore be passed directly
to other `dbsnR` functions.

A study area extending 5 km around Orvinio can be created with:

```{r}
orvinio_5km <- dbsn_buffer(
  x = orvinio,
  distance = 5000
)
```

# Merge all available layers

When the `layer` argument is omitted, `dbsn_merge()` processes all
available DBSN layers.

```{r}
dbsn <- dbsn_merge(
  province = provinces
)
```

The result is a named list of `sf` objects.

```{r}
names(dbsn)
```

Each element corresponds to one DBSN layer.

For example:

```{r}
dbsn$loc_sg
dbsn$bosco
dbsn$tr_str
```

The number of features in each merged layer can be inspected with:

```{r}
sapply(dbsn, nrow)
```

# Filter features by attributes

`dbsn_filter()` filters features of an individual `sf` layer while
preserving geometry.

For example, features belonging only to Rieti can be selected with:

```{r}
rieti <- dbsn_filter(
  loc_sg,
  province = "RI"
)
```

Multiple values can be supplied for the same attribute.

```{r}
rieti_aquila <- dbsn_filter(
  loc_sg,
  province = c("RI", "AQ")
)
```

Values within the same attribute are interpreted as alternatives.

Conditions involving different attributes are combined.

```{r}
selected <- dbsn_filter(
  loc_sg,
  province = "RI",
  loc_sg_sgn = c("01", "04")
)
```

Character comparisons can also be made case-insensitive.

```{r}
selected <- dbsn_filter(
  loc_sg,
  loc_sg_top = "montasola",
  ignore_case = TRUE
)
```

# Select thematic layers

A complete DBSN dataset can contain many layers.

`dbsn_select()` extracts only the layers required for a particular
analysis.

```{r}
territory <- dbsn_select(
  x = dbsn,
  layers = c(
    "loc_sg",
    "edifc",
    "tr_str",
    "el_vms",
    "bosco",
    "cl_agr",
    "scarpt"
  )
)
```

The selected layers can be inspected with:

```{r}
names(territory)
```

and their number of features with:

```{r}
sapply(territory, nrow)
```

Working with only the required thematic layers can considerably reduce
the amount of spatial data that must be processed during subsequent
analyses.

# Define a study point

A study location can also be represented using geographic coordinates.

```{r}
study_point <- st_sfc(
  st_point(
    c(12.9, 42.13)
  ),
  crs = 4326
)
```

The coordinates are specified as:

```text
longitude, latitude
```

The input coordinates in this example use WGS84 (`EPSG:4326`).

# Create a study area

`dbsn_buffer()` creates an area around an `sf` or `sfc` spatial object.

A study area extending 20 km around the point can be created with:

```{r}
study_area <- dbsn_buffer(
  x = study_point,
  distance = 20000
)
```

The distance is expressed in metres.

When geographic coordinates are supplied, `dbsn_buffer()` transforms
the input to a projected coordinate reference system before calculating
the buffer.

The resulting geometry can be inspected with:

```{r}
study_area
st_crs(study_area)
```

# Crop a single DBSN layer

`dbsn_crop()` can crop an individual `sf` object.

```{r}
loc_sg_crop <- dbsn_crop(
  x = loc_sg,
  area = study_area
)
```

The effect of the crop can be inspected by comparing the number of
features.

```{r}
nrow(loc_sg)
nrow(loc_sg_crop)
```

# Crop multiple DBSN layers

`dbsn_crop()` can also operate directly on a named list produced by
`dbsn_select()` or `dbsn_merge()`.

```{r}
territory_crop <- dbsn_crop(
  x = territory,
  area = study_area
)
```

The number of retained features can then be inspected for every layer.

```{r}
sapply(territory_crop, nrow)
```

A useful comparison is:

```{r}
data.frame(
  layer = names(territory),
  before = sapply(territory, nrow),
  after = sapply(territory_crop, nrow)
)
```

# Intersecting versus clipping

By default, `dbsn_crop()` uses:

```{r}
method = "intersects"
```

This retains complete features whenever they intersect the study area.

For example, a road entering the study area is kept as a complete
feature.

If geometries must instead be physically cut at the study-area
boundary, use:

```{r}
territory_clip <- dbsn_crop(
  x = territory,
  area = study_area,
  method = "clip"
)
```

This distinction makes it possible to choose between feature selection
and exact geometric clipping depending on the analysis.

# Crop with a bounding box

A rectangular area can also be defined directly using longitude and
latitude.

```{r}
area <- st_bbox(
  c(
    xmin = 12.8,
    ymin = 42.0,
    xmax = 13.2,
    ymax = 42.4
  ),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
)
```

The bounding box can then be supplied directly to `dbsn_crop()`.

```{r}
loc_sg_bbox <- dbsn_crop(
  x = loc_sg,
  area = area
)
```

The cropping area is automatically transformed to the coordinate
reference system of the DBSN layer.

# Spatial operations

`dbsnR` provides wrappers for common spatial operations while
preserving standard `sf` objects.

## Spatial intersection

Features intersecting another spatial object can be obtained with:

```{r}
objects_intersecting <- dbsn_intersect(
  loc_sg,
  study_area
)
```

## Spatial join

Attributes from spatially related objects can be combined using:

```{r}
joined <- dbsn_join(
  loc_sg,
  study_area
)
```

## Geometric difference

A geometry can be subtracted from another spatial dataset with:

```{r}
difference <- dbsn_difference(
  territory_crop$bosco,
  study_area
)
```

## Geometric union

Spatial geometries can be combined with:

```{r}
combined <- dbsn_union(
  territory_crop$bosco
)
```

These functions complement `dbsn_crop()` when an analysis requires
topological operations rather than spatial selection alone.

# Corridors along linear features

`dbsn_corridor()` creates a corridor along a linear feature.

For example, a corridor extending 500 m on each side of a road can be
created with:

```{r}
road_corridor <- dbsn_corridor(
  road,
  distance = 500
)
```

Spatial objects can also be selected directly within the corridor.

```{r}
objects_in_corridor <- dbsn_corridor(
  road,
  distance = 500,
  objects = loc_sg,
  relation = "intersects"
)
```

This can be used to analyse settlements, buildings, archaeological
features, or other spatial objects located along roads and other linear
features.

# Nearest features

`dbsn_nearest()` identifies the nearest reference feature for each input
feature.

```{r}
nearest <- dbsn_nearest(
  loc_sg,
  tr_str
)
```

When the actual distance is required, `dbsn_distance()` calculates the
minimum distance to the nearest reference feature.

```{r}
distance <- dbsn_distance(
  x = loc_sg,
  y = tr_str
)
```

The original geometry is preserved and distance information is added to
the result.

# Locate features along a line

`dbsn_along()` locates spatial features along a reference line.

Features are projected onto the line and their position is calculated
from the start of the line.

```{r}
along <- dbsn_along(
  line = road,
  objects = loc_sg
)

along[, c(
  "distance_m",
  "distance_km",
  "distance_pct"
)]
```

The function adds three attributes:

- `distance_m`: distance from the start of the line in metres;
- `distance_km`: distance from the start of the line in kilometres;
- `distance_pct`: relative position along the line from 0 to 100.

The direction of the reference line determines the origin of the
measurement: 0 represents the start of the LINESTRING and 100 represents
its end.

# Spatial measurements

Linear feature lengths can be calculated with `dbsn_length()`.

```{r}
roads_length <- dbsn_length(
  tr_str
)
```

Measurements in metres and kilometres are added to the result.

Polygon areas can be calculated with `dbsn_area()`.

```{r}
forest_area <- dbsn_area(
  bosco
)
```

The original geometry is preserved together with the calculated
measurements.

# Contour lines

DBSN contour lines are stored in the `cv_liv` layer.

They can be merged across the study provinces in the same way as other
DBSN layers.

```{r}
cv_liv <- dbsn_merge(
  layer = "cv_liv",
  province = provinces
)
```

The elevation associated with each contour line is stored in
`cv_liv_q`.

For a local analysis, only contour lines around Orvinio can be retained.

```{r}
cv_orvinio <- dbsn_intersect(
  cv_liv,
  orvinio_5km
)
```

Restricting large line datasets to the study area before interactive
visualisation improves map responsiveness and avoids unnecessarily
rendering features outside the area of interest.

# Interactive maps

Individual DBSN layers can be displayed with `dbsn_map()`.

```{r}
dbsn_map(
  orvinio,
  basemap = "topo",
  hover = "loc_sg_top"
)
```

The function automatically handles point, line, and polygon geometries.

Spatial features can also be coloured according to a numeric or
categorical attribute.

For example, the contour lines around Orvinio can be coloured according
to elevation.

```{r}
dbsn_map(
  cv_orvinio,
  basemap = "topo",
  color_by = "cv_liv_q",
  hover = "cv_liv_q"
)
```

Numeric attributes use a continuous colour scale, while categorical
attributes use discrete colours.

# Multiple-layer maps

Several spatial layers can be displayed together using
`dbsn_map_layers()`.

```{r}
dbsn_map_layers(
  cv_orvinio,
  orvinio,
  orvinio_5km,
  basemap = "topo",
  layer_names = c(
    "Contour lines",
    "Orvinio",
    "5 km buffer"
  ),
  colors = c(
    "#8C510A",
    "#E31A1C",
    "#2166AC"
  )
)
```

Each spatial object is added as an independent Leaflet layer and can be
shown or hidden using the layer control.

This makes it possible to combine DBSN thematic data, analysis results,
buffers, corridors, and study-area boundaries in a single interactive
map.

# Summarise a layer

A compact summary of a DBSN layer can be generated using
`dbsn_summary()`.

```{r}
dbsn_summary(
  loc_sg,
  layer = "loc_sg"
)
```

This provides a quick overview of the spatial dataset before subsequent
analysis or export.

# Export spatial layers

The final dataset can be exported using `dbsn_export()`.

A named list of `sf` objects can be written to a single GeoPackage, with
each list element becoming a separate GeoPackage layer.

```{r}
dbsn_export(
  x = territory_crop,
  file = "study_area_dbsn.gpkg"
)
```

The resulting GeoPackage can be opened directly in GIS software such as
QGIS.

Existing files are protected by default.

To replace an existing GeoPackage explicitly:

```{r}
dbsn_export(
  x = territory_crop,
  file = "study_area_dbsn.gpkg",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
```

A single `sf` object can also be exported.

```{r}
dbsn_export(
  x = loc_sg_crop,
  file = "loc_sg_study_area.gpkg",
  layer = "loc_sg"
)
```

# Complete workflow

A complete `dbsnR` workflow can be written compactly as follows.

```{r}
library(dbsnR)
library(sf)

# Provinces

provinces <- c(
  "RI",
  "AP",
  "AQ",
  "PG",
  "RM",
  "TE",
  "TR",
  "VT"
)

# Merge settlement/locality layer

loc_sg <- dbsn_merge(
  layer = "loc_sg",
  province = provinces
)

# Locate Orvinio

orvinio <- dbsn_search(
  x = loc_sg,
  pattern = "Orvinio"
)

# Create a 5 km study area

orvinio_5km <- dbsn_buffer(
  x = orvinio,
  distance = 5000
)

# Merge contour lines

cv_liv <- dbsn_merge(
  layer = "cv_liv",
  province = provinces
)

# Select contour lines in the study area

cv_orvinio <- dbsn_intersect(
  cv_liv,
  orvinio_5km
)

# Display contour lines by elevation

dbsn_map(
  cv_orvinio,
  basemap = "topo",
  color_by = "cv_liv_q",
  hover = "cv_liv_q"
)

# Display multiple spatial layers

dbsn_map_layers(
  cv_orvinio,
  orvinio,
  orvinio_5km,
  basemap = "topo",
  layer_names = c(
    "Contour lines",
    "Orvinio",
    "5 km buffer"
  ),
  colors = c(
    "#8C510A",
    "#E31A1C",
    "#2166AC"
  )
)

# Export results

results <- list(
  orvinio = orvinio,
  study_area = orvinio_5km,
  contour_lines = cv_orvinio
)

dbsn_export(
  x = results,
  file = "orvinio_dbsn.gpkg"
)
```

# Workflow overview

The principal `dbsnR` workflow is:

```text
dbsn_download()
       |
       v
Cache
       |
       v
dbsn_layers() / dbsn_info()
       |
       v
dbsn_merge()
       |
       v
dbsn_search() / dbsn_filter() / dbsn_select()
       |
       v
dbsn_buffer() / dbsn_crop() / dbsn_corridor()
       |
       v
dbsn_intersect() / dbsn_join()
dbsn_difference() / dbsn_union()
       |
       v
dbsn_nearest() / dbsn_distance() / dbsn_along()
       |
       v
dbsn_length() / dbsn_area()
       |
       v
dbsn_summary()
       |
       v
dbsn_map() / dbsn_map_layers()
       |
       v
dbsn_export()
```

This workflow makes it possible to move from provincial DBSN
geodatabases to a reproducible spatial analysis covering data
acquisition, caching, thematic selection, spatial processing,
measurement, interactive visualisation, and export.

All major processing functions return standard `sf` objects whenever
possible, allowing `dbsnR` results to be used directly with `sf`,
`dplyr`, `ggplot2`, `leaflet`, QGIS, and other spatial tools.
